linkedin.title: This Week in Finance & Tech
linkedin.body:
The landscape of technology and science shifted significantly this week. Here are the developments you should know.

In the consumer tech space, Apple has made its biggest design change since 2007. The company unveiled the iPhone Duo, a folding, passport-sized device priced near $2,000. It marks the first major product test for new CEO John Ternus. Meanwhile, if you are planning to test out new software, remember that installing an iOS public beta requires a full data backup first to ensure your information remains secure.

Hardware constraints are impacting medical innovation. The head of chip designer Arm noted that a shortage of chips is currently slowing down AI research aimed at cancer treatment. While computers are expected to eventually solve complex DNA modelling, current capacity is limiting progress.

In the aerospace sector, a German startup called Isar Aerospace successfully launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe. This is a critical step for Europe as it tries to build independent access to space. On a larger scale, astronomers just released the most detailed map of the universe ever made. It covers 75 percent of the sky and features 4 billion celestial objects. Not to be outdone by Earth, Saturn has also revealed another mysterious, perfect geometric shape in its atmosphere, adding to the list of phenomena scientists are still working to understand.

Finally, in sustainability and automotive news, a new study offers good news for electric vehicle owners. Data suggests that EV batteries retain about 90 percent of their original capacity even after 150,000 km of driving. In the UK, a unique restoration project at Emblehope Moor is testing a new model for land acquisition. The plan aims to provide financial returns to investors before transferring ownership to community or charitable groups.

reels.title: Cell wall transport disruption exposes weakness in antibiotic-resistant bacteria
reels.hook: Cell wall transport disruption exposes weakness in antibiotic-resistant bacteria

beats.caption: Cell wall transport disruption exposes weakness in antibiotic-resistant bacteria
Imagine your front door lock is broken.
beats.narration: Imagine your front door lock is broken and you cannot keep anyone out. That is bacterial defense.

beats.caption: Bacteria usually block our best antibiotics.
beats.narration: Usually, antibiotic-resistant bacteria are experts at keeping medicine out. They have strong walls to block them.

beats.caption: Scientists found a hidden weakness inside.
beats.narration: But researchers at Umeå University just found a hidden weakness inside that protective wall.

beats.caption: Disrupting the transport system changes everything.
beats.narration: They discovered that disrupting the cell's transport system makes the bacteria vulnerable again.

beats.caption: This new strategy could bypass resistance.
beats.narration: So, instead of banging on the front door, scientists could theoretically target the delivery system inside.

beats.caption: Better ways to treat infections.
beats.narration: This insight might help researchers create entirely new ways to treat infections that currently resist drugs.

beats.narration: For more science updates, check out headlinne.com. How do you think we should solve antibiotic resistance?

story_card.standfirst: New open-source software makes lunar data accessible for everyone.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text: NASA and IBM released new open-source software to help people map the moon.

steps.label: How we got here
steps.text: The two organizations combined their resources to make satellite data easier to use.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.text: Researchers can now study the lunar surface more easily for scientific discovery.

story_card.caption:
NASA and IBM have released open source lunar mapping tools for public use.

By opening up these tools, the agencies are making it simpler for researchers and developers to analyze satellite data. It is a big step toward democratizing space science and helping us learn more about our closest neighbor.
